text: András Hodanics / Age: 29
Rank/Position: Corporal (junior non-commissioned officer), squad leader
Civilian Occupation: Mason
Origin: Bácska / Southern Hungary (Vojvodina)
Hodanics András would have paid a serious sum — if he'd ever possessed the kind of money that
deserves the word “serious” — for someone to explain to him how the hell he ended up here.
He knew every step of the road to the Don, obviously.
He could recite it half-asleep. The medical exam in Sombor. The training after that in Baja.
The endless train ride to the East. And the final, soul-crushing march into the Big Nowhere that crowned the whole ordeal.
So the logistics made sense to him. What didn't make sense was the “why”.
Why he had to stand here and kill men he didn't even know?
Men who had lived half a world away from him.
Men who, for all he could tell, were just as clueless about the point of this entire
ordeal as he was.
He vaguely remembered that some powerful country had attacked another, less powerful
country, and that the leaders of other, more powerful countries hadn't liked it.
But how that chain of events led to him putting down his mason's trowel to pick up a rifle
instead… this remained a mystery to him.
Maybe it didn't even matter.
Maybe it was a waste of thought. But he just couldn't stop.
He had been a sensitive boy his whole life.
Not the kind who threw around big words,
but the kind who couldn't help wondering what human dignity is measured in.
He pretended otherwise, of course. He had to. A mason's son doesn't get to be delicate.
Not openly. In the pub he had to throw punches like the rest of them. At the pig
slaughter, he had to grip the knife as hard as his uncles and cousins.
He learned to look hard, even when he wasn't.
So why now — an enemy of war in principle, a man who
hates the very idea of it — why does he clutch the barrel of his rifle the way a drowning
man clutches a rope? Because, after years of searching, he had finally found someone
in front of whom he didn't have to pretend. Someone who could accept him as he was.
And to get back to that person,
he first had to trample his own values into the mud.
He had to put down at least as many Soviets
as the bricks he had once stacked proudly,
building a house for the woman he loved.
That's how he met her.
She had asked him, together with her husband,
to build them a house in the center of his hometown. A long-term contract and good pay, a mason's dream…
but her eyes. Gray, almost transparent. The way she looked him over the first time, like
she could see into his soul.
At first, he told himself he imagined it. That he was flattering himself.
But summer came.
He worked outside in the sun until his shirt clung to him.
And Elza stepped out from the neighboring house where she lived with her husband's parents.
She brought him cold beer.
She took a teasing sip from it herself.
And once the beer loosened their tongues, they started to talk.
Those conversations began in awkwardness,
but before he knew it, he was opening up to her the way he had never opened up before to anyone.
Trying to seduce a married woman would have been dangerous.
And András didn't think he even had the stomach for it.
But Elza's husband had been taken for training a year before András.
And a few months later, a letter arrived.
He was dead.
He wasn't coming home.
Elza mourned him, yes.
But András couldn't help noticing how little devotion there was
in it, how quickly the grief seemed to turn into something else.
He took it as a sign. A sign for their future.
Still, out of decency, he meant to wait.
Let the dark weeks pass. Let the widowhood be widowhood.
Let time do its work. But the world didn't wait for him.
The war didn't adjust itself to his conscience. Things bigger than him, things that grew over his
head, reached down and grabbed him and turned his life upside down. And then, the whim of fate
tossed him here, to the end of the earth.
Hodanics András aims. He asks the Almighty for forgiveness.
Then he squeezes the trigger.
After the shot, he shifts his weight from one foot to the other, afraid that the ring,
hidden in his underwear, will slip and fall out. The ring his mother gave him. The ring he carried
nearly two thousand kilometers. The ring he meant to use to ask Elza to marry him.
He can't let it hit the ground.
Not here.
Not on this ice.
Red with blood.
